findings.issue: Residual (now narrower) keystroke race, reproduced live for the first time this round. The _inputSeq guard correctly stops a superseded handler from emitting a stale Value, but OnAfterRenderAsync still writes the winning handler's _pendingValue into the DOM unconditionally, and that write can land AFTER further characters have already been typed into the element — erasing them. Reproduced in the running host (Wakeel.Desktop, /gallery, real Input.dispatchKeyEvent keystrokes over CDP) twice: on the very first interaction after a page load, dispatching 1,2,0,9,2,0,2,6 with zero delay produced "12/06" once and "12/09/206" once (digits silently dropped). At any measurable inter-keystroke delay it is correct: 5 ms, 15 ms, 25 ms, 40 ms, 80 ms and 150 ms all produced "12/09/2026" with caret 10, warm and cold. So this is not reachable by a human at a keyboard (Windows key auto-repeat is ~30 ms) and not reachable by paste (one input event); it needs literally simultaneous keystrokes on a cold component. Recording it so the hazard is not lost, not as a blocker.
findings.fix: Make the post-render DOM write conditional on the element still holding the text the handler actually processed. In OnDateInputAsync stash the raw text alongside the pair (`_pendingRaw = raw;`), pass it as a fourth argument from OnAfterRenderAsync (`Js.InvokeVoidAsync("wakeelUi.setInputValue", _dateRef, value, caret, expectedRaw)`), and in wakeelUi.setInputValue (src/Wakeel.Design/wwwroot/js/app.js) return early when `expected !== undefined && el.value !== expected`, so a write whose input the DOM has already moved past becomes a no-op instead of clobbering newer characters. Keep the existing clamp. Add a bUnit test mirroring DateType_OutOfOrderInteropReplies_... that asserts the stale write is skipped.

findings.issue: DateType_OutOfOrderInteropReplies_SupersededKeystrokeIsDroppedNotEmittedStale relies on cut.WaitForAssertion(() => Assert.Single(... setInputValue ...)) as its synchronization point. The assertion it waits on is a count that is also transiently true in the regression case (without the _inputSeq guard the first continuation produces exactly one invocation before the second one lands), so the wait can release early; the test still fails correctly in that case, but on the following Assert.Equal(new[]{"12"}, values) rather than on the count, and the wait condition is not a monotone one. Not a defect today (with the guard in place exactly one invocation can ever occur, so the test is stable), just a fragile synchronization choice.
findings.fix: Wait on the terminal, monotone condition instead: cut.WaitForAssertion(() => Assert.Equal(new[] { "12" }, values)); then assert Assert.Single(JSInterop.Invocations, i => i.Identifier == "wakeelUi.setInputValue") and its (value, caret) arguments afterwards.

SECURITY — CLEAN. getSelectionStart(el) reads only el.selectionStart on the ElementReference it is handed; setInputValue(el, value, caret) assigns only el.value on that same reference and clamps with Math.max/Math.min before setSelectionRange. The password path never touches either helper, so no secret crosses the interop boundary, reaches a log, the database or UI state. Identifiers, comments and XML docs are English; no password, key or seed is held anywhere.
